## Problem 1 - OOP Programming

Create a class to represent Wald-style normal approximation Confidence Intervals. Do this using S4.

### a) Define the waldCI class.

#### A constructor, which takes in a confidence level (0,1) and either a mean and standard error, or a lower and upper bound. This should be a custom constructor, not new() or waldCI().

#### A validator.

```{r}

setClass("waldCI", slots = c(
  level = "numeric",
  mean = "numeric",
  sterr = "numeric",
  lb = "numeric",
  ub = "numeric"
  ))

setValidity("waldCI", function(object) {
  
  has_level <- length(object@level) == 1
  if (!has_level) {
    stop("level cannot be empty.")
  }
  
  if (object@level > 1) {
    stop("level too high")
  }
  if ( length(object@level) == 1 && object@level < 0) {
    stop("level too high")
  }
  
  if (length(object@sterr) == 1 && object@sterr < 0) {
    stop ("can't have a negative sterr")
  }
  if (length(object@lb) == 1 && length(object@ub) == 1 && object@lb > object@ub) {
    stop("can't have lb greater than ub")
  }
  if (length(object@lb) == 1 && length(object@ub) == 1 && object@lb == Inf) {
    stop("can't have infinite lb")
  }
  if (length(object@lb) == 1 && length(object@ub) == 1 && object@ub == Inf) {
    stop("can't have infinite ub")
  }
  
  has_mean <- length(object@mean) == 1
  has_sterr <- length(object@sterr) == 1
  has_lb <- length(object@lb) == 1
  has_ub <- length(object@ub) == 1
  
  option_1 <- has_mean & has_sterr
  option_2 <- has_lb & has_ub
  
  
  if (option_1 | option_2) {
    return(TRUE)
  } else {
    stop("needs mean and sterr or lb and ub")
  }
  
})


```

#### A show method.

```{r}

setMethod("show", "waldCI",
  function(object) {
    cat(paste("The confidence level: ", object@level))
    cat("\n")
    cat(paste("The mean: ", object@mean))
    cat("\n")
    cat(paste("The standard error: ", object@sterr))
    cat("\n")
    cat(paste("The lower bound: ", object@lb))
    cat("\n")
    cat(paste("The upper bound: ", object@ub))
    cat("\n")
    return(invisible(object))
  }
)

```

#### A contains method, returning a logical of whether a value is within a CI.

```{r}
setGeneric("contains",
           function(object, value) {
             standardGeneric("contains")
           })

setMethod("contains", "waldCI",
  function(object, value) {
    
  has_mean <- length(object@mean) == 1
  has_sterr <- length(object@sterr) == 1
  has_lb <- length(object@lb) == 1
  has_ub <- length(object@ub) == 1
    
    option_1 <- has_mean & has_sterr
    option_2 <- has_lb & has_ub
    
    if (option_1) {
      lb <- object@mean - (2 * object@sterr)
      ub <- object@mean - (2 * object@sterr)
      return(value > lb & value < ub)
    } else {
      return(value > object@lb & value < object@ub)
    }
  }
)
```

#### An overlap method, that takes in two waldCI’s, and returns a logical of whether the two confidence intervals overlap.

```{r}
setGeneric("overlap", function(object_one, object_two) {
  standardGeneric("overlap")
})

setMethod("overlap",
          signature = c(object_one = "waldCI", object_two = "waldCI"),
  function(object_one, object_two) {
    
    has_mean <- length(object_one@mean) == 1
    has_sterr <- length(object_one@sterr) == 1
    has_lb <- length(object_one@lb) == 1
    has_ub <- length(object_one@ub) == 1
    
    option_1 <- has_mean & has_sterr
    option_2 <- has_lb & has_ub
    
    lb_one <- 0
    ub_one <- 0
    
    if (option_1) {
      lb_one <- object_one@mean - (2 * object_one@sterr)
      ub_one <- object_one@mean - (2 * object_one@sterr)
    } else {
      lb_one <- object_one@lb
      ub_one <- object_one@ub
    }
    
    has_mean <- length(object_two@mean) == 1
    has_sterr <- length(object_two@sterr) == 1
    has_lb <- length(object_two@lb) == 1
    has_ub <- length(object_two@ub) == 1
    
    option_1 <- has_mean & has_sterr
    option_2 <- has_lb & has_ub
    
    lb_two <- 0
    ub_two <- 0
    
    if (option_1) {
      lb_two <- object_two@mean - (2 * object_two@sterr)
      ub_two <- object_two@mean - (2 * object_two@sterr)
    } else {
      lb_two <- object_two@lb
      ub_two <- object_two@ub
    }
    
      overlap <- ((lb_one > lb_two & lb_one < ub_two) | (ub_one > lb_two & ub_one < ub_two) | (lb_two > lb_one & lb_two < ub_one) | (ub_two > lb_one & ub_two < ub_one))
  
  return(overlap)
      
  })
  

```

#### as.numeric to return c(lb, ub). (Hint: The second argument of setGeneric is not needed when an existing s3 function uses the .Primitive function.)

```{r}
setMethod("as.numeric",
          signature = c(x = "waldCI"),
  function(x) {
    return(c(x@lb, x@ub))
})
```

#### transformCI which takes in a function and a waldCI, and returns the transformed waldCI object. Warn the user that only monotonic functions make sense.

```{r}
setGeneric("transformCI", function(object, fn) {
  standardGeneric("transformCI")
})

setMethod("transformCI",
          signature = c(object = "waldCI"),
  function(object, fn) {
    
  has_mean <- length(object@mean) == 1
  has_sterr <- length(object@sterr) == 1
  has_lb <- length(object@lb) == 1
  has_ub <- length(object@ub) == 1
  
  option_1 <- has_mean & has_sterr
  option_2 <- has_lb & has_ub
  
  if (option_1) {
    return(new("waldCI", level = object@level, mean = fn(object@mean), sterr = fn(object@sterr)))
  } else {
    return(new("waldCI", level = object@level, lb = fn(object@lb), ub = fn(object@ub)))
  }
  
})

```

### c)

```{r}
result <- tryCatch(
  expr = {
    x <- new("waldCI", confidence_level = 0.9, mean = 2, sterr = -2)
  },
  error = function(e) {
    print(e)
    print("Validated an error occurred for negative standard error.")
  }
)

result <- tryCatch(
  expr = {
    x <- new("waldCI", confidence_level = 0.9, lb = 2, ub = 1)
  },
  error = function(e) {
    print(e)
    print("Validated an error occurred for lb > ub.")
  }
)

result <- tryCatch(
  expr = {
    x <- new("waldCI", confidence_level = 0.9, lb = 2, ub = Inf)
  },
  error = function(e) {
    print(e)
    print("Validated an error occurred for Infinite bounds.")
  }
)

result <- tryCatch(
  expr = {
    x <- new("waldCI", confidence_level = 0.9, lb = 2, ub = 3)
    ub(x) <- 1
  },
  error = function(e) {
    print(e)
    print("Validated an error occurred for invalid setter.")
  }
)

```

## Problem 2 - data.table

# Use the “ATP Matches” data from 2019.

```{r}
library(data.table)
tennis <- fread("tennis-atp-sackmann-data/atp_matches_2019.csv")
```

### a) How many tournaments took place in 2019?

```{r}

print(class(tennis))

# We see that it is a data.table type

print(paste("The 2019 number of tournaments was",
            length(unique(tennis$tourney_id))))

```

However, there were multiple Davis cup finals.
```{r}

tourneys <- unique(tennis[, .(tourney_name)])

tourneys[str_detect(tourney_name, "Davis Cup")][1:5]
```



```{r}
nrow(tourneys[, tourney_name := sub("Davis.*", "Davis Cup", tourney_name)][, .N, by = tourney_name][, N := NULL])
```

So there are only 69 unique tournaments.

### b) Did any player win more than one tournament? If so, how many players won more than one tournament, and how many tournaments did the most winning player(s) win?

```{r}
tennis <- fread("tennis-atp-sackmann-data/atp_matches_2019.csv")

multiwinners <- tennis[order(tourney_name, -match_num), .SD[1], by = tourney_name][, .(wins = .N), by = winner_name][wins > 1][order(-wins)]

nrow(multiwinners)
```
There are 17 winners who won multiple tournaments. 
```{r}
multiwinners %>%
  slice(1:2)
```
Rafael Nadal won the most, at 9 tournaments.

### c) Is there any evidence that winners have more aces than losers? (If you address this with a hypothesis test, do not use base R functionality - continue to remain in the Tidyverse.)

```{r}
library(tidymodels)

tennis %>%
  select(w_ace, l_ace) %>%
  mutate(win_more = w_ace > l_ace) %>%
  prop_test(win_more ~ NULL, p = .5)
```
Therefore, yes we have statistical significant evidence that winners perform more aces than losers.

### d) Identify the player(s) with the highest win-rate. (Note that this is NOT asking for the highest number of wins.) Restrict to players with at least 5 matches.

```{r}
tennis <- fread("tennis-atp-sackmann-data/atp_matches_2019.csv")

tennis_matches_winner_count <- tennis[, .(wins = .N), by = winner_name]
tennis_matches_loser_count  <- tennis[, .(losses = .N), by = loser_name]

tennis_win_lose_count <- merge(
  tennis_matches_winner_count, 
  tennis_matches_loser_count, 
  by.x = "winner_name", 
  by.y = "loser_name", 
  all = TRUE
)

tennis_win_lose_count <- tennis_win_lose_count[wins + losses >= 5][, ratio := wins / (wins + losses)][order(-ratio)]

print(head(tennis_win_lose_count, 5))
```
One player has the highest win-rate, and it is again Rafael Nadal.

## Problem 3 - plotly

```{r}
data <- read_csv("us-states.csv")

```

# a) How many major and minor spikes in cases were there?

```{r}

data$date <- lubridate::ymd(data$date)

names(data)[names(data) == "date"] <- "Date"
names(data)[names(data) == "state"] <- "State"

library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

g <- ggplot(data, aes(x = Date, y = cases_avg)) +
  geom_line(color = "red", linewidth = 1.1) + 
  labs(
    title = "COVID Daily Case Numbers.",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily Cases"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
    
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 14),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "grey", size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "darkgrey")
  )

ggplotly(g)
```

There are 4 minor spikes and 4 major spikes. 


# b) For the states with the highest and lowest overall rates per population, what differences do you see in their trajectories over time?

```{r}

data <- read_csv("us-states.csv")


state_rates <- aggregate(
  cases_avg_per_100k ~ state,
  data = data,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  FUN = sum
)

extremes <- state_rates$state[
  state_rates$cases_avg_per_100k %in%
    range(state_rates$cases_avg_per_100k)
]

trajectory <- data[data$state %in%
                     extremes, ]
trajectory <- trajectory[order(trajectory$date), ]

data$date <- as.Date(data$date)

g <- data[data$state %in%
       extremes, ] |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date,
             y = cases_avg_per_100k,
             color = state)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = paste("Daily case rates: ",
                  paste(extremes, collapse = ", ")),
    x = "Date",
    y = "Cases per 100,000",
    color = "State"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(g)
```

Overall, they tend to spike at the same times, but Rhode Island spikes bigger. Other differences include that the spike in winter 21-22 did not seem to affect Maine, while it increased rates by a factor of 10 in Rhode Island.


### c) Identify, to the best of your ability without a formal test, the first five states to experience COVID in a substantial way.

```{r}
data <- read_csv("us-states.csv")
data$date <- lubridate::ymd(data$date)

names(data)[names(data) == "date"] <- "Date"
names(data)[names(data) == "state"] <- "State"

data20 <- data %>%
  filter(year(Date) == 2020) %>%
  select(State, Date, cases_avg_per_100k)

g <- ggplot(data20, aes(x = Date, y = cases_avg_per_100k, color = State)) + geom_line() + ylab("COVID cases per 100k") + theme(legend.position = "off")

ggplotly(g)
```
Now we zoom in.

```{r}
data20 <- data20 %>%
  filter(month(Date) %in% c(3, 4, 5)) # Mar-May
g <- ggplot(data20, aes(x = Date, y = cases_avg_per_100k, color = State)) +
  geom_line() +
  ylab("COVID cases per 100k")

ggplotly(g)
```

As covid came in a single starting wave and spread, we can deduce it from the graph. We look at the first 5 that had an average of greater than 1 per 100K.

```{r}

data <- read_csv("us-states.csv",
                 show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))

first_substantial <- data %>%
  filter(cases_avg_per_100k >= 1) %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  filter(!(state  %in%
             c("Guam", "District of Columbia"))) %>%
  slice_min(date,
            n = 1,
            with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

first_substantial %>%
  select(state,
         date,
         cases_avg_per_100k)

top_5_states <- first_substantial %>%
  pull(state)

g <- data %>%
  filter(state %in%
           top_5_states,
         date >= as.Date("2020-01-01"),
         date <= as.Date("2020-3-31")) %>%
  group_by(state, date) %>%
  summarise(total_cases = sum(cases,
                              na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date,
             y = total_cases,
             color = state,
             group = state)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "COVID Cases.",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Number of Cases",
    color = "State"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 14),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "grey", size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "darkgrey"),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
    legend.title = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(color = "darkgrey")
  )

ggplotly(g)
```


Therefore, we conclude that Washington, Louisiana, Michigan, New Jersey, and New York were the first five states to experience COVID in a significant way.
